title: Unit 3: Exercise 3 - The Lost City of DeMille Emerges from the Desert Sands of California

parts.title: Part 1
parts.content:
1 For 75 years, the majestic dunes that tower over this humble coastal village have held one of Hollywood's oldest and strangest secrets.


2 Cecil B. DeMille, a founding father of motion pictures, once chose this remote, wind-swept site 170 miles (270 kilometres) north of Los Angeles to erect a plaster replica of ancient Egypt and stage his 1923 silent epic "The Ten Commandments." It had all the right touches, on a monumental scale — from the walls of a pharaoh's city rising 10 stories high to an avenue of nearly two dozen five-ton sphinxes lining the sand. There had never been anything like it, and it remains one of the largest movie sets ever built.


3 But once the cameras stopped rolling and a cast of thousands sent packing, it all vanished. Then in his memoirs, DeMille dropped a playful hint of the historic set's mysterious fate. "If 1,000 years from now, archaeologists happen to dig beneath the sands of Guadalupe," he wrote, "I hope they will not rush into print with the amazing news that Egyptian civilization, far from being confined to the Valley of the Nile, extended all the way to the Pacific Ocean of North America."


4 They will not. Because now, in an only-in-California endeavour as sublime as it is ridiculous, what's left of the lost city of DeMille may soon be saved by an authentic archaeological dig like none other.


5 That all of the Egyptian relics to be excavated are fake hardly matters, at least not to the small and zealous band of filmmakers and archaeologists leading the unusual project, or to the curious towns around here that are beginning to help pay for it. Inside the new Dunes Discovery Center along the creaking and dusty old main street of Guadalupe (population 6,000), some worn, fragile DeMille props that already have been discovered are even being displayed reverently in glass cases, as if they were priceless artifacts.


6 "Digging up a fake Egyptian city in California is hard to do without laughing, I know," said Peter Brosnan, 46, a documentary filmmaker who has made the buried set his abiding pastime. "But this is an important piece of early 20th-century American history. It's about the only set left from the era of silent film. We know it's down there in the sand, and we think it's mostly intact."


7 Chunks of artful plaster are not all they are after. The sheer size of DeMille's production also makes it a rich time capsule preserved in a mountain of sand, with abundant emblems of daily life from the 1920s. Something always turns up when the sands shift, such as cough syrup bottles once used to hold sips of alcohol.


8 To make the film, DeMille marched an army of 2,500 actors from Los Angeles and kept them captive there for two months in an elaborate tent city assembled on the 18-mile stretch of dunes. More than 1,500 construction workers also came to build the mammoth biblical set.


9 DeMille, who remade the film in the 1950s in Egypt with Charlton Heston playing Moses, even hired musicians to lug instruments into the sands of Guadalupe and play for the huge cast as it worked. But their performances on the set ended one day when a runaway horse-drawn chariot crashed into the orchestra pit.


10 "At first I thought that doing a real dig for this was a little strange," said John Parker, an archaeologist who has worked extensively at the dunes. "In order not to destroy this stuff we have to use the same techniques we would use as if this was a 10,000-year-old prehistoric site. But along with the film history we find, it could be a great way to see what life was like here in the 1920s."


11 By the time he was finished, DeMille had spent $1.4 million filming the biblical epic, a huge sum at the time. And he was way over budget. Mr. Brosnan said he suspects that DeMille buried the set because it was the cheapest option he had. Other film historians contend that he also may have been worried that another director would sneakily use it and release a similar movie faster.


12 Archaeologists are convinced that more than one third of the film set is long gone, ravaged by time and the powerful forces of nature along the ocean here. But after using ground-penetrating radar to probe the dunes, some of which slope as high as 500 feet (150 metres), they believe they finally know exactly where everything that's left has been entombed. Many of the sphinxes, as well as several 35-foot statues of a pharaoh king that DeMille put outside the walls of his phony Egyptian city seem fairly well preserved, they said.


13 "They really did a good job hiding it," said Liz Scott-Graham, the programme manager at the Dunes Discovery Center, the non-profit group that owns the dunes and treats them like a nature preserve. "You would never know it's all still there."

questions.content: Which of the following is true?
options: A. Buried under the dunes are priceless Egyptian relics.
B. The city is Hollywood's oldest movie set.
C. Egyptian civilization actually extended to North America.
D. Although a replica, the city is now considered archaeologically important.
questions.answer: D. Although a replica, the city is now considered archaeologically important.
questions.explanation: Đáp án D đúng. Trong đoạn 4, tác giả nói rằng những gì còn sót lại của "thành phố DeMille" sắp được cứu vãn bởi một cuộc khai quật khảo cổ thực sự ("saved by an authentic archaeological dig"). Đồng thời ở đoạn 6, nhà làm phim tài liệu Peter Brosnan nhấn mạnh: "But this is an important piece of early 20th-century American history. It's about the only set left from the era of silent film." Điều này cho thấy mặc dù chỉ là một bản sao, nhưng khu phim trường này hiện nay được coi là có tầm quan trọng về mặt khảo cổ học.

questions.content: Why did DeMille build the Egyptian city?
options: A. To shoot "The Ten Commandments".
B. To build a tourist resort.
C. To commemorate a pharaoh.
D. To study Egyptian culture.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A đúng. Thông tin nằm ở đoạn 2: "Cecil B. DeMille... chose this remote, wind-swept site... to erect a plaster replica of ancient Egypt and stage his 1923 silent epic 'The Ten Commandments'." Nghĩa là ông đã dựng nên bản sao thành phố Ai Cập cổ đại này để làm bối cảnh quay bộ phim câm "Mười điều răn" (The Ten Commandments) vào năm 1923.

questions.content: Why did archaeologists dig up the dunes?
options: A. To look for Egyptian relics.
B. To shoot a documentary.
C. To save the DeMille city.
D. To study the history of motion pictures.
questions.answer: C. To save the DeMille city.
questions.explanation: Đáp án C đúng. Thông tin nằm ở đoạn 4: "... what's left of the lost city of DeMille may soon be saved by an authentic archaeological dig like none other." (những gì còn sót lại của thành phố DeMille bị mất tích có thể sớm được cứu vãn bởi một cuộc khai quật khảo cổ thực sự chưa từng có). Nghĩa là mục đích của cuộc khai quật này là để cứu/bảo tồn khu phim trường DeMille.

questions.content: Filmmakers and archaeologists show interest in the site
options: A. because they could study people's life in the 1920s.
B. because they could study how films were made in the 1920s.
C. because they wanted to know how the city was built.
D. because they wanted to remake the film.
questions.answer: A. because they could study people's life in the 1920s.
questions.explanation: Đáp án A đúng. Thông tin được nhắc đến ở đoạn 7: "... a rich time capsule preserved in a mountain of sand, with abundant emblems of daily life from the 1920s." và ở đoạn 10, nhà khảo cổ học John Parker nói: "... along with the film history we find, it could be a great way to see what life was like here in the 1920s." Cả nhà khảo cổ học và nhà làm phim đều quan tâm đến di chỉ này vì ngoài lịch sử điện ảnh, nó giống như một "viên nang thời gian" giúp họ tìm hiểu về cuộc sống thường ngày vào những năm 1920.

questions.content: The following statements are true except
options: A. DeMille buried the set because he didn't want others to use it.
B. DeMille did not finish the film because of the budget and had to remake it in the 1950s.
C. DeMille buried the set because it was the cheapest way.
D. DeMille used more than 4,000 people in building the set and making the film.
questions.answer: B. DeMille did not finish the film because of the budget and had to remake it in the 1950s.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B đúng vì đây là câu phát biểu sai (câu hỏi yêu cầu tìm ý không đúng). Trong đoạn 11 nói rằng "By the time he was finished, DeMille had spent $1.4 million filming the biblical epic...", nghĩa là ông đã hoàn thành bộ phim câm này, dù bị vượt ngân sách rất nhiều. Việc ông làm lại (remade) bộ phim vào những năm 1950 (nhắc đến ở đoạn 9) không phải vì bộ phim cũ chưa hoàn thành do thiếu ngân sách. Các ý còn lại đều đúng: A và C đúng (đoạn 11 giải thích lý do chôn lấp: "cheapest option" và lo sợ đạo diễn khác lén lút sử dụng "another director would sneakily use it"), D đúng (đoạn 8: "army of 2,500 actors" cộng "More than 1,500 construction workers" tổng cộng hơn 4,000 người).

questions.content: What happened to the buried city?
options: A. More than one third of the city is damaged by the powerful forces of nature.
B. The city was so well hidden that nearly everything remains intact.
C. Part of the city has been used by other filmmakers.
D. Most of the city is long gone.
questions.answer: B. The city was so well hidden that nearly everything remains intact.
questions.explanation: Đáp án B. Trong đoạn 6, Peter Brosnan cho biết: "We know it's down there in the sand, and we think it's mostly intact" (Chúng tôi biết nó nằm dưới cát, và chúng tôi nghĩ rằng nó hầu như còn nguyên vẹn). Đoạn 13 cũng nhắc lại lời của Liz Scott-Graham: "They really did a good job hiding it... You would never know it's all still there" (Họ đã giấu nó rất kỹ... Bạn sẽ không bao giờ biết rằng tất cả vẫn còn ở đó). Dù đoạn 12 có nói hơn một phần ba khu phim trường đã biến mất, nhưng nhiều bức tượng nhân sư và tượng pharaoh vẫn "fairly well preserved" (được bảo tồn khá tốt), và những người khai quật vẫn tin rằng phần lớn khu vực giấu kín vẫn còn nguyên vẹn.
